kan_hizmeti_2026_11_05.title: Cyberattack disrupts blood storage refrigeration systems in France
kan_hizmeti_2026_11_05.full_text:
France's national blood service has confirmed that a cyberattack targeting a refrigeration equipment provider raised temperature and defrost settings at three of its facilities, threatening stored blood products.

The French Blood Establishment (Établissement français du sang or EFS), which manages blood collection, processing, and distribution across France, said the incident occurred on November 2 and affected systems used to monitor and control cold-storage chambers.

According to a statement published on November 3, EFS was not directly targeted in the cyberattack, but was instead its refrigeration supplier.

While EFS has not named the affected supplier, European refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld Rentals confirmed in a statement that a cybersecurity incident involving remote monitoring software had affected a limited number of its refrigeration units.

Coolworld says the attackers exploited a vulnerability in a third-party component, which was outside the company's direct control.

"The vulnerability currently being reported in the media relates to a component from a third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control," the company said.

"Only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected, and Coolworld responded promptly and took appropriate measures."

The company said it is working with affected customers but will not comment on individual cases.

At EFS, the incident raised temperature and defrost thresholds in affected cold-storage chambers to extremely high levels.

These facilities store blood products before they are distributed to hospitals, as well as biological samples maintained by the EFS.

EFS says its monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the temperature change, allowing staff to fix impacted equipment or transfer products to other refrigeration facilities.

"No health impact has been identified, and no loss of blood products has been reported," EFS said in its statement [translated from French].

abd_ussleri_2026_10_30.full_text:
US Probes Suspected Hack Behind Military Base Freezer Failures

The Pentagon treats August freezer failures at US military bases as a suspected hack and is working with French investigators after a supermarket attack.

The Pentagon is investigating freezer failures that spoiled food at US military bases in August as a suspected cyberattack, according to four officials who spoke to Reuters. One official said US investigators are also in contact with French authorities about a similar attack on commercial freezers that disrupted supermarkets in France earlier this month. This is the first time Reuters has reported that the US incident is being treated as a suspected cyberattack.

“The Pentagon is ​treating the spate of mysterious freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at military bases across the United States in August as a suspected hack, according to four officials familiar ‌with the matter.” Reuters reports.

“One of the officials said the military investigators were in touch with their French counterparts about a similar cyberattack on commercial freezers that disrupted supermarkets there earlier this month.”

It is still unclear who is behind the attacks. Reuters could not determine how far the investigation has progressed or whether investigators have identified the cause or those responsible. The Pentagon said a unit of US Cyber Command is working closely with other government agencies and law enforcement. The Army’s Criminal Investigation Division confirmed that its Cyber Field Office is involved and is working with French law enforcement to investigate the freezer outages in Europe.

The incidents hit commissaries, the on-base stores where military personnel buy food. At least six were affected in late August, according to Reuters’ review of the bases’ Facebook posts and website updates. Stars and Stripes named Fort Irwin, F.E. fransa_market_2026_10_16.full_text:
Supermarket Refrigeration Attack Widens to Copeland, Dixell Controllers

Roughly 700 French supermarkets were hit by the cyberattacks, for which no group has claimed responsibility.

The cyberattack that disrupted refrigeration at hundreds of French supermarkets this week also affected equipment from Copeland and its Dixell brand, according to France’s national cybersecurity agency ANSSI.
ANSSI’s CERT-FR first warned on October 12 of numerous compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series refrigeration controllers. A day later, the agency updated its alert to include Copeland XWEB and Dixell XWEB systems.



Copeland initially declined to confirm the agency’s findings, but it has since acknowledged a vulnerability. “We are currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk,” the company said.



This summer, Claroty detailed flaws in Danfoss’s AK-SM 800A, along with 23 vulnerabilities in Copeland’s XWEB Pro controller. Copeland patched them in a firmware update.



It is still unclear how the attackers gained access. The CERT-FR alert does not link the compromises to any specific vulnerability, and neither Danfoss nor French authorities have tied the attack to the flaws Claroty disclosed.



Danfoss said most of the affected devices are older AK-SM 800 and AK-SC 355 systems, which have reached end of life and are no longer patched. The vendor stopped supporting the AK-SM 800 in May 2021, and the AK-SC 355 was discontinued in 2016. binance_2026_10_30.title: Binance pauses withdrawals as hackers suspected of stealing billions in crypto
binance_2026_10_30.full_text:
Binance has confirmed to TechCrunch that it is dealing with a security incident as users reported that funds were being drained from the crypto exchange’s wallets.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch that it is “aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.”

“Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” Binance said in a statement.

“Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information,” the statement added. “Users should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.”

Binance spokesperson Ross O’Leary said that Binance has “temporarily suspended withdrawals on multiple networks following a security incident as a precautionary measure.”

News of the breach comes hours after Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said in a post on X that the company likely had been hacked. Zhao, who no longer runs the company but is its largest shareholder, said that he expects users’ funds to be “fully covered” but did not provide an explanation for the claim.

Financial tech giant Circle froze about $800 million in Tether as it passed through its networks, while crypto giant Tether froze about $1.56 billion related to Binance’s hack.

Crypto watchers say at least $2 billion has been drained from Binance’s hot wallets, which are internet-connected cryptocurrency wallets that store crypto that are connected to the internet. By some estimates, Binance may have lost upward of $5.7 billion in crypto, though the numbers have not been confirmed and it’s possible that the theft is ongoing.

It’s unclear who is behind the hack, and Binance did not say if it had received any correspondence from the hackers.

bitget_2026_10_01.title: Bitget Confirms Third-Party Zero-Day Behind $387.5 Million Cryptocurrency Theft
bitget_2026_10_01.full_text:
Cryptocurrency exchange Bitget on Wednesday confirmed that attackers who stole $387.5 million last week exploited a zero-day flaw in third-party security products, citing ongoing investigation findings from SlowMist.

"Their investigation identified malicious activity involving third-party security products, including a zero-day vulnerability, and recovered a customized tool used by the attacker to initiate unauthorized withdrawals," Bitget said in a post on X.

On September 24, 2026, the cryptocurrency exchange disclosed that threat actors stole $387.5 million from its hot and warm wallets through a series of unauthorized transfers, prompting it to halt all withdrawals temporarily. Close to $1.1 million in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen by Circle, Tether, and NEAR Intents.

In a subsequent analysis, Bitget said the attackers exploited the flaw to obtain high-level internal credentials and use them to issue fraudulent withdrawal commands to the wallet system and initiate "abnormal transfers that bypassed existing risk controls." Bitget has since notified the relevant third-party vendor and disabled the affected functionality pending completion of a fix.

The incident impacted 11 blockchains, including Ethereum, XRP Ledger, Zcash, TRON, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, BNB Smart Chain, Avalanche, Algorand, and Celestia. Affected assets identified to date include XRP, ETH, USDT, ZEC, ATOM, USDC, USD0, XAUt, BNB, AVAX, TRX, ALGO, and TIA.
